title: A red tower, then a red circle
label: Brand gallery
lede: For most of its life a Circuit City was recognizable from the road by a red entrance tower. The last generation of stores wore a round red logo instead. Here are both as they survive in photographs and the archive, with our drawings in the same spirit.

archive.caption: The round logo used in the final years, from the website header.
archive.credit: Cropped from an Internet Archive capture of circuitcity.com. Shown for commentary; trademarks belong to their owners.

archive.caption: A later-format store with the round logo on a yellow panel.
archive.credit: Photo: Staus at English Wikipedia, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Circuitcity1.jpg), public domain.

archive.caption: The older format: the red tower entrance on a closed store in Newington, Connecticut.
archive.credit: Photo: Mike Kalasnik, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Circuit_City_Newington,_CT_%286935749475%29.jpg), CC BY-SA 2.0.

archive.caption: A “Going out of business” banner on a later-format store during the liquidation.
Inside a store ten days before the sales ended: “Store closing sale,” “Everything must go,” “All sales final.”
archive.credit: Photo: Ildar Sagdejev (Specious), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:2009-02-26_Circuit_City_store_closing_everything_must_go.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0.

drawings.title: The superstore.
drawings.caption: A showroom in front, a warehouse behind and a red tower over the door.

drawings.title: The 48-hour disc.

drawings.title: The wage management initiative.

drawings.caption: The signs that hung in 567 stores from January 17, 2009.[^15]
